addmaths-0606-trig-exact-values.description: Use the unit circle to find the value and sign of sine, cosine and tangent in degrees or radians.

sections.title: How does an angle become a point on a circle?
sections.label: Unit circle

blocks.html: Start from the positive horizontal axis. The point reached on a unit circle is \((\cos x,\sin x)\).

figure.alt: Unit circle with an arrow in the second quadrant and dotted projections to its negative horizontal and positive vertical components.
figure.caption: Cosine is the horizontal coordinate and sine is the vertical coordinate. Here cosine is negative and sine is positive.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Imagine a stick of length one rotating about the origin. Looking at its tip, read the signed horizontal position first and the signed vertical position second. The horizontal entry gives cosine and the vertical entry gives sine. Angles drawn anticlockwise are positive. Angles drawn clockwise are negative. Add or subtract \(360^\circ\) to bring an angle to a familiar direction without moving its final point.

blocks.title: Read an exact trigonometric value
blocks.hint: Mark the angle on a unit circle before deciding on its sign.
blocks.solution:
After removing whole turns, evaluate \(\sin\left(180^\circ\right)\).

The angle is on one of the axes. Read the coordinates directly from the unit circle.

Sine has exact value \(0\).

Answer: \(0\).

blocks.html: Both legs of an ordinary triangle have positive lengths. Coordinates in other quadrants can be negative, so the trig values can also be negative.

blocks.title: Read an exact trigonometric value
blocks.hint: Mark the angle on a unit circle before deciding on its sign.
blocks.solution:
After removing whole turns, evaluate \(\cos\left(0\right)\).

The angle is on one of the axes. Read the coordinates directly from the unit circle.

Cosine has exact value \(1\).

Answer: \(1\).

retry.feedback: The reference value has the correct magnitude. Check the sign in this quadrant.

blocks.html: Leave exact values in fractions or surds. Use angle units only on angles.

sections.title: How can special triangles give exact values?
sections.label: Reference

blocks.html: A reference angle is the small positive angle between the final direction and the horizontal axis. Use the special triangles for \(30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: For \(45^\circ\), equal legs and Pythagoras give a hypotenuse \(\sqrt2\) times a leg. For \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\), split an equilateral triangle in half. The short leg, long leg and hypotenuse have ratio \(1:\sqrt3:2\). The triangle supplies the size. Read the sign from the actual quadrant. With a point on an axis, read its coordinates from the circle instead of drawing a triangle.

blocks.title: Read an exact trigonometric value
blocks.hint: Mark the angle on a unit circle before deciding on its sign.
blocks.solution:
After removing whole turns, evaluate \(\tan\left(30^\circ\right)\).

The reference angle is \(30^\circ\). Use the signs of the coordinates in the actual quadrant.

Tangent has exact value \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

Answer: \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

retry.feedback: The reference value has the correct magnitude. Check the sign in this quadrant.

blocks.html: The tangent is the quotient \(\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\). Avoid reversing the ratio.

blocks.title: Read an exact trigonometric value
blocks.hint: Mark the angle on a unit circle before deciding on its sign.
blocks.solution:
After removing whole turns, evaluate \(\cos\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)\).

The reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Use the signs of the coordinates in the actual quadrant.

Cosine has exact value \(- \frac{1}{2}\).

Answer: \(- \frac{1}{2}\).

retry.feedback: The reference value has the correct magnitude. Check the sign in this quadrant.

blocks.html: Leave exact values in fractions or surds. Use angle units only on angles.

sections.title: Which unit am I working in?
sections.label: Radians

blocks.html: A half-turn can be named \(180^\circ\) or \(\pi\) radians. The rotation and trig value are unchanged.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Check the unit stated in the question before entering an angle on a calculator. To move from degrees to radians, multiply by pi and divide by 180. To move back, reverse the conversion. Keep a radian answer in terms of pi when the question asks for exact values. The same quadrants and signs still apply. A negative angle can also be moved forward by whole turns.

blocks.title: Switch angle units
blocks.hint: Use the conversion factor that cancels the given unit.
blocks.solution:
A half-turn is both \(180^\circ\) and \(\pi\) radians.

Multiply by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\) and simplify.

Answer: \(495^\circ\).

blocks.html: An angle measured in radians does not carry the degree symbol. In a mixed comparison, convert both angles before deciding which is larger.

blocks.prompt: Given \(\cos x=-\frac{20}{29}\) and \(\frac{5 \pi}{2}
blocks.hint: Use the unit-circle identity to get the square, then decide the sign separately.
blocks.solution:
Use \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\). The two square roots have the same positive magnitude.

The interval places the angle in quadrant 2, so choose the positive value.

Answer: \(\frac{21}{29}\).

retry.feedback: The magnitude is right. Check whether the angle is above or below the horizontal axis.

addmaths-0606-trig-periodic-graphs.description: Draw and read sine, cosine and tangent, including their zeros, repeats and differences.

sections.title: Where should I begin a trig sketch?
sections.label: Landmarks

blocks.html: Mark the values at quarter turns first. The sine graph starts at zero and the cosine graph starts at its maximum.

figure.alt: Sine and cosine graphs across one turn, with ticks every quarter turn.
figure.caption: Sine (blue) starts at zero. Cosine (orange) starts at its maximum.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Draw a horizontal angle axis and a vertical value axis. Use evenly spaced quarter-turn marks. Follow the unit-circle coordinates through one turn to plot the first curve. For sine, the coordinate goes up, back to zero, down and back to zero. For cosine, the coordinate starts at the right-hand edge of the circle, which gives its maximum. Join the plotted points with a smooth curve and use a ruler for the axes.

blocks.title: Read a point on a basic graph
blocks.prompt: The graph is \(y=\cos\left(x\right)\). Find its exact ordinate at \(x=675^\circ\).
blocks.hint: Start with the angle and read up or down to the curve.
blocks.solution:
Move along the horizontal axis to the given angle. The repeat distance is \(360^\circ\).

Reducing the input to one cycle gives the ordinate \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

Answer: \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

blocks.html: A sine graph starting at its maximum has the cosine starting point. Read the name before drawing.

blocks.title: Read an exact trigonometric value
blocks.hint: Mark the angle on a unit circle before deciding on its sign.
blocks.solution:
After removing whole turns, evaluate \(\sin\left(\frac{7 \pi}{6}\right)\).

The reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Use the signs of the coordinates in the actual quadrant.

Sine has exact value \(- \frac{1}{2}\).

Answer: \(- \frac{1}{2}\).

retry.feedback: The reference value has the correct magnitude. Check the sign in this quadrant.

blocks.html: Label the angle units on your horizontal axis before adding quarter-turn marks.

sections.title: What does one period look like?
sections.label: Repeat

blocks.html: The period is the smallest positive horizontal distance that gives the same complete shape again.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Choose matching points facing the same direction. Two successive rising zeros of sine are one whole cycle apart. A rising zero and the next falling zero are separated by only half a cycle. In a formula with a scaled angle, start from the basic period and divide by the angle multiplier.

FunctionFull period in degreesFull period in radians
Sine or cosine\(360^\circ\)\(2\pi\)
Tangent\(180^\circ\)\(\pi\)

blocks.title: Find the horizontal period
blocks.prompt: Find the period of the graph \(y=6\sin\left(\frac{5}{6}x\right)-3\) in radians.
blocks.hint: Find how much the argument must change for one full repeat. Divide by its input multiplier.
blocks.solution:
One full repeat of sine takes \(2 \pi\) in the argument.

The input multiplier is \(\frac{5}{6}\). Divide the original period by \(\frac{5}{6}\).

Answer: \(\frac{12 \pi}{5}\).

retry.feedback: That is the period before changing the horizontal scale.

blocks.html: Two identical y-values can lie on different parts of the same cycle. Check the local direction or a matching peak.

blocks.title: Read a point on a basic graph
blocks.prompt: The graph is \(y=\cos\left(x\right)\). Find its exact ordinate at \(x=- \frac{19 \pi}{6}\).
blocks.hint: Start with the angle and read up or down to the curve.
blocks.solution:
Move along the horizontal axis to the given angle. The repeat distance is \(2 \pi\).

Reducing the input to one cycle gives the ordinate \(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

Answer: \(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

blocks.html: Label the angle units on your horizontal axis before adding quarter-turn marks.

sections.title: Why does tangent leave gaps?
sections.label: Tangent

blocks.html: Tangent is \(\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\). The curve is undefined where cosine is zero and repeats every half-turn.

figure.alt: Three tangent branches, separated at the dashed vertical lines at 90 and 270 degrees.
figure.caption: The tangent curve approaches a vertical asymptote from either side. Leave a gap between branches.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Use the denominator to find an asymptote. Draw a dashed vertical line there before sketching the curve. Between two asymptotes, tangent runs through all real values. Through its zeros the curve rises, on both sides of a quarter-turn it approaches different ends of the y-axis, and across the asymptote it breaks. For sine and cosine a scale changes the height, but for tangent there is no greatest or least y-value.

blocks.title: Label the vertical asymptotes
blocks.prompt: Give the x-coordinates of all vertical asymptotes of \(y=4\tan\left(4x\right)-2\) for \(- \frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi}{4}\).

field.label: All values of x (comma separated, in the stated unit)

blocks.hint: Find where the cosine in the denominator vanishes. The vertical shift does not alter these x-coordinates.
blocks.solution:
The graph is undefined where the cosine of the argument is zero.

Within a full period, the argument is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=4x\) is \(- 2 \pi\le u\le\pi\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Answer: \(x=- \frac{3 \pi}{8},\quad - \frac{\pi}{8},\quad \frac{\pi}{8}\).

retry.feedback: You found one solution. Check the other symmetry angle and then sweep the entire interval.

blocks.html: Do not join tangent across an asymptote. The angle there has no value of tangent.

blocks.title: Find the x-intercepts
blocks.prompt: Find all x-intercepts of \(y=8\sin\left(\frac{5}{6}x\right)\) for \(- 3 \pi\le x\le - \frac{3 \pi}{5}\). Give the x-coordinates.

field.label: All values of x (comma separated, in the stated unit)

blocks.hint: Set the y-value to zero and solve for the angle inside the function.
blocks.solution:
A non-zero scale \(8\) leaves the zeros unchanged.

Within a full period, the argument is \(0\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=\frac{5}{6}x\) is \(- \frac{5 \pi}{2}\le u\le- \frac{\pi}{2}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Answer: \(x=- \frac{12 \pi}{5},\quad - \frac{6 \pi}{5}\).

retry.feedback: You found one solution. Check the other symmetry angle and then sweep the entire interval.

solution: Move along the horizontal axis to the given angle. The repeat distance is \(2 \pi\).
Reducing the input to one cycle gives the ordinate \(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

examples.title: Find the horizontal period
examples.question: Find the period of the graph \(y=8\tan\left(\frac{3}{4}x\right)+1\) in degrees.
solution: One full repeat of tangent takes \(180^\circ\) in the argument.
The input multiplier is \(\frac{3}{4}\). Divide the original period by \(\frac{3}{4}\).
Answer: \(240^\circ\).

examples.title: Read a point on a basic graph
examples.question: The graph is \(y=\cos\left(x\right)\). Find its exact ordinate at \(x=\frac{8 \pi}{3}\).
solution: Move along the horizontal axis to the given angle. The repeat distance is \(2 \pi\).
Reducing the input to one cycle gives the ordinate \(- \frac{1}{2}\).

examples.title: Label the vertical asymptotes
examples.question: Give the x-coordinates of all vertical asymptotes of \(y=6\tan\left(3x\right)+3\) for \(-60^\circ\le x\le 90^\circ\).
solution: The graph is undefined where the cosine of the argument is zero.
Within a full period, the argument is \(90^\circ\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(180^\circ\).
The given interval for the full argument \(u=3x\) is \(-180^\circ\le u\le270^\circ\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.
Answer: \(x=-30^\circ,\quad 30^\circ,\quad 90^\circ\).

examples.title: Find the x-intercepts
examples.question: Find all x-intercepts of \(y=4\sin\left(\frac{5}{6}x\right)\) for \(- \frac{9 \pi}{5}\le x\le \frac{3 \pi}{5}\). Give the x-coordinates.
solution: A non-zero scale \(4\) leaves the zeros unchanged.
Within a full period, the argument is \(0\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).
The given interval for the full argument \(u=\frac{5}{6}x\) is \(- \frac{3 \pi}{2}\le u\le\frac{\pi}{2}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.
Answer: \(x=- \frac{6 \pi}{5},\quad 0\).

addmaths-0606-trig-scaled-waves.description: Sketch a scaled and shifted wave, read its range and recover amplitude, midline and period.

sections.title: How do height and midline work together?
sections.label: Height

blocks.html: For \(y=a\sin(bx)+c\) with positive \(a\), the extrema are \(c-a\) and \(c+a\). The cosine version follows the same rule.

figure.alt: Comparison of basic sine and a sine wave with twice the frequency, a larger amplitude and a shifted midline.
figure.caption: Doubling the angle creates two cycles. The shifted blue curve oscillates either side of its dotted midline.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Put a dotted line at y equal to the vertical shift. This is the centre of the wave. The amplitude is the step from the centre to a peak or a trough. If the maximum and minimum are given instead, their mean gives the midline and half their difference gives the amplitude. This also tells you how to find a missing vertical scale from a graph.

blocks.title: Read a maximum from the midline
blocks.hint: Work upwards from the midline by one amplitude.
blocks.solution:
The midline is \(y=-1\). The amplitude is \(7\).

The maximum is \(-1+7=6\).

Answer: \(6\).

retry.feedback: That is the amplitude. Add it to the value on the midline.

blocks.html: The amplitude is half the full vertical height. The highest y-value also includes the midline shift.

blocks.title: Recover amplitude from two extremes
blocks.prompt: A cosine curve has minimum \(-3\) and maximum \(5\). Find its amplitude.
blocks.hint: The full height covers two equal amplitude steps.
blocks.solution:
The vertical distance between its extrema is \(8\).

Only half that distance is above the midline. Divide by \(2\).

Answer: \(4\).

retry.feedback: This is peak-to-trough height, which is twice the amplitude.

blocks.html: Show the endpoints and one full repeat clearly. Use enough vertical scale to label the midline and extrema.

sections.title: How do I move the quarter-turn landmarks?
sections.label: Speed

blocks.html: The inside multiplier \(b\) controls the horizontal scale. A complete sine or cosine cycle takes \(\frac{360^\circ}{b}\) or \(\frac{2\pi}{b}\) for positive \(b\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Use the expression inside the brackets for the angles on the usual wave. Solve a short equation for the x-coordinate of each point. For a sketch, begin with the ends of one cycle and divide that distance into four equal parts. Scale the ordinate and apply the vertical shift. sections.label: Reciprocals

blocks.html: Secant is \(\frac{1}{\cos x}\). Cosecant is \(\frac{1}{\sin x}\). Cotangent is \(\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\).

figure.alt: Unit circle with an arrow in the second quadrant and dotted projections to its negative horizontal and positive vertical components.
figure.caption: Cosine is the horizontal coordinate and sine is the vertical coordinate. Here cosine is negative and sine is positive.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Read the familiar sine or cosine coordinate first. Take a reciprocal only after making sure its denominator is not zero. For cotangent, the quotient of the two coordinates works whenever sine is non-zero. You can also take the reciprocal of tangent on their common domain when tangent is non-zero. At the top of the unit circle, cosine is zero and sine is one, so cotangent is zero even though tangent is undefined.

sections.title: How can I choose between the three identities?

blocks.html: Start from \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\). Dividing by cosine squared produces the secant and tangent identity. Dividing by sine squared produces the cosecant and cotangent identity.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: The choice depends on the two squared functions in the question. For a squared secant use \(\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x\). For a squared cosecant use \(\operatorname{{cosec}}^2x=1+\cot^2x\). Dividing by a squared factor still requires that factor to be non-zero. If the question asks for a function value and not its square, choose a sign using information about the quadrant.

blocks.title: Use an identity to find a squared value
blocks.hint: Choose the identity containing the given squared function and the target.
blocks.solution:
Use \(\sec^2u=1+\tan^2u\).

Square \(1\) before substituting it. The square removes any negative sign.

Answer: \(2\).

blocks.html: Match the related pair before rearranging. A tangent term goes with secant, and a cotangent term goes with cosecant.

blocks.prompt: The product \((7\operatorname{cosec}\left(x+\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right)+7\cot\left(x+\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right))(7\operatorname{cosec}\left(x+\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right)-7\cot\left(x+\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right))\) is constant throughout its domain. Find that constant.
blocks.hint: Name the repeated argument u. Expand the two conjugate brackets before choosing an identity.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the conjugate brackets using the difference of two squares.

Factor out \(49\). The remaining difference is one by the cosecant and cotangent identity.

Both terms in the original brackets have denominator \(\sin\left(x+\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right)\). Exclude its zeros.

Answer: \(49\).

How are the other three functions defined?

Secant is \(\frac{1}{\cos x}\). Cosecant is \(\frac{1}{\sin x}\). Cotangent is \(\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\).

How can I choose between the three identities?

Start from \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\). Dividing by cosine squared produces the secant and tangent identity. Dividing by sine squared produces the cosecant and cotangent identity.

Can I solve by using the reciprocal?

After isolating a reciprocal trig function, switch to sine or cosine and find its base angles. Treat a zero cotangent separately.

    Answer. \(x=180^\circ,\quad 360^\circ,\quad 1260^\circ\).

addmaths-0606-trig-identity-proofs.description: Prove identities by rewriting one side, using exact algebra and stating where the original expression exists.

sections.title: Which side should I start with?
sections.label: Starting

blocks.html: Choose the side with more terms, more brackets or more fractions. Rewrite that side one step at a time until it matches the other.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: List what the target uses before you start. If it contains sine and cosine, rewrite tangents and reciprocals in terms of those coordinates. If there are squares, check whether the identity \(\sin^2u+\cos^2u=1\) can turn a difference into a single term. Start from an existing side and show equal expressions line by line.

blocks.title: Recognise a constant trigonometric expression
blocks.prompt: Find the constant value of \(114\left(\sec^2\left(\frac{3}{8}x\right)-\tan^2\left(\frac{3}{8}x\right)\right)\) throughout its domain.
blocks.hint: Look for the difference between a squared reciprocal and its related squared function.
blocks.solution:
\(1+\tan^2u=\sec^2u\) holds where \(\cos u\ne0\).

Subtract the squared tangent term. The factor in brackets is one.

Answer: \(114\).

blocks.html: Testing one angle supports a check but cannot prove an identity for all allowed angles.

blocks.title: Use two identities independently
blocks.prompt: Find the constant value of \(\frac{\sec^2\left(4x\right)-\tan^2\left(4x\right)}{118}+1\left(\sin^2\left(4x\right)+\cos^2\left(4x\right)\right)\) throughout its domain.
blocks.hint: Treat the numerator and the second pair as two different Pythagorean identities.
blocks.solution:
Use \(\sec^2u-\tan^2u=1\) to simplify the numerator.

Use \(\sin^2u+\cos^2u=1\) to simplify the product.

The final value is \(\frac{1}{118}+1=\frac{119}{118}\).

Answer: \(\frac{119}{118}\).

blocks.html: A sum and a difference of the same terms multiply to a difference of squares. Factor out any common coefficient before using a trig identity.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: If the squared terms are secant and tangent at the same argument, their difference is one. Cosecant and cotangent give the same result. Use a new letter to name a complicated shared argument. After simplifying, replace the letter with the given argument. Keep the condition that the denominator of the original terms is non-zero.

blocks.title: Use an identity to find a squared value
blocks.hint: Choose the identity containing the given squared function and the target.
blocks.solution:
Use \(\cos^2u=1-\sin^2u\).

Square \(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) before substituting it. The square removes any negative sign.

Answer: \(\frac{1}{4}\).

blocks.html: The square of a sum is not the sum of squares. Use the difference-of-squares rule only for matching conjugates.

sections.title: How do I prove an identity with several denominators?
sections.label: Fractions

blocks.html: Rewrite in two basic coordinates, combine the numerator first and cancel only a non-zero factor.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Start with the allowed values. Turn reciprocal expressions into fractions with sine or cosine denominators. Rewrite an expression subtracted from its reciprocal over a single denominator. Often the new numerator is one minus the square of one coordinate, which switches it to the other coordinate squared. Now write the divisor as a fraction and multiply by its reciprocal. Keep the original restrictions even when all denominators cancel.

blocks.title: Find the coefficient in a quotient identity
blocks.prompt: The expression \(\frac{5\sec\left(x+225^\circ\right)-5\cos\left(x+225^\circ\right)}{\tan\left(x+225^\circ\right)}\) simplifies to \(k\sin\left(x+225^\circ\right)\) on its domain. Find \(k\).
blocks.hint: Begin with the side containing the quotient. Rewrite the numerator and the divisor before cancelling.

Write the reciprocal in terms of sine or cosine. The numerator becomes \(\frac{5(1-\cos^2\left(x+225^\circ\right))}{\cos\left(x+225^\circ\right)}\).

examples.title: Use an identity to find a squared value
examples.question: It is known that \(u=2940^\circ\) and \(\cot\left(u\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Find \(\operatorname{cosec}^2u\).
solution: Use \(\operatorname{cosec}^2u=1+\cot^2u\).
Square \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\) before substituting it. The square removes any negative sign.
Answer: \(\frac{4}{3}\).

revision.body:
Which side should I start with?

Choose the side with more terms, more brackets or more fractions. Rewrite that side one step at a time until it matches the other.

When does factorising make a proof shorter?

A sum and a difference of the same terms multiply to a difference of squares. Factor out any common coefficient before using a trig identity.

How do I prove an identity with several denominators?

Rewrite in two basic coordinates, combine the numerator first and cancel only a non-zero factor.
